```{webr}
#| include: false
#| autorun: true
# Lab machinery – the pre-computed specification universe and the helper
# functions the exercise flow uses. Participants interact with try_spec(),
# my_experiments(), submit_exploration(), prereg(), build_model(),
# run_spec() and report_result(); every result they print comes from the
# committed grid of 2,520 pre-computed specifications, so no heavy model
# fitting happens in the browser.
.grid <- read.csv("data/spec_grid_full.csv")
.neg_framings <- c("mcomm", "mlib", "mneg")

.menu <- list(
  my_outcome     = c("mcosmo", "mutil", "mcomm", "mlib", "mpos", "mneg"),
  my_family      = c("gaussian", "beta"),
  my_predictor   = c("unemp", "growth"),
  my_pred_form   = c("raw", "log"),
  my_copredictor = c("none", "growth", "unemp"),
  my_estimator   = c("fe_twoway", "fe_country", "re", "pooled_cl"),
  my_sample      = c("all", "y2004_2008", "y2009_2013", "no_bailout", "no_GR_ES"),
  my_weights     = c("none", "n_cy")
)

.est_lab <- function(e) c(
  fe_twoway  = "two-way fixed effects (country + year)",
  fe_country = "country fixed effects",
  re         = "random effects",
  pooled_cl  = "pooled OLS, clustered by country")[[e]]

# Menu validation, shared by both routes into the grid: the exploratory
# try_spec(), which takes its choices as arguments, and the declared flow,
# which reads them from the participant's preregistration cell. Keeping one
# validator means an error message a participant learns in Task 4 is the same
# message they meet in Task 5.
.validate <- function(ch, as_args = FALSE) {
  for (k in names(.menu)) {
    v <- ch[[k]]
    # try_spec() names its arguments `outcome`, `estimator` and so on; the
    # preregistration cell names the same choices `my_outcome`, `my_estimator`.
    # Report back whichever name the participant actually typed.
    shown <- if (as_args) sub("^my_", "", k) else k
    if (!is.character(v) || length(v) != 1 || !v %in% .menu[[k]])
      stop(sprintf("%s = \"%s\" is not on the menu. Options: %s.",
                   shown, paste(v, collapse = ","),
                   paste(.menu[[k]], collapse = " | ")), call. = FALSE)
  }
  if (ch$my_estimator == "re" && ch$my_weights == "n_cy")
    stop("The random-effects estimator is never fitted with weights (the menu excludes re + n_cy). Use weights = \"none\" or pick another estimator.",
         call. = FALSE)
  if (ch$my_predictor == "growth" && ch$my_pred_form == "log")
    stop("GDP growth enters raw only – it takes negative values, so the log is undefined. Use pred_form = \"raw\".",
         call. = FALSE)
  if (ch$my_predictor == ch$my_copredictor)
    stop(sprintf("%s is already your claim-carrying predictor; the copredictor must be \"none\" or the other measure.",
                 ch$my_predictor), call. = FALSE)
  ch
}

.check_choices <- function() {
  need <- names(.menu)
  missing <- need[!vapply(need, exists, logical(1))]
  if (length(missing) > 0)
    stop("Not declared yet: ", paste(missing, collapse = ", "),
         ". Fill in every choice in the preregistration cell and run it first.",
         call. = FALSE)
  if (!exists("claim_align"))
    stop("Also declare claim_align <- TRUE (the day's convention) in the preregistration cell.",
         call. = FALSE)
  ch <- lapply(need, function(k) get(k))
  names(ch) <- need
  .validate(ch)
}

.lookup <- function(ch) {
  hit <- .grid[.grid$outcome == ch$my_outcome & .grid$family == ch$my_family &
               .grid$predictor == ch$my_predictor &
               .grid$pred_form == ch$my_pred_form &
               .grid$copredictor == ch$my_copredictor &
               .grid$estimator == ch$my_estimator &
               .grid$sample == ch$my_sample & .grid$weights == ch$my_weights, ]
  if (nrow(hit) != 1)
    stop("That combination is not in the pre-computed universe – check each choice against the menu comments.",
         call. = FALSE)
  hit
}

# the claim-alignment factor: negative framings are reverse-coded (1 - y),
# and growth's claim-expected sign is positive, so both flip the sign
.flip <- function(ch, hit)
  (if (hit$positive_outcome) 1 else -1) *
  (if (ch$my_predictor == "growth") -1 else 1)

.spec_line <- function(ch) {
  neg <- ch$my_outcome %in% .neg_framings
  paste0(ch$my_outcome, if (neg) "_ca" else "", " ~ ",
         ch$my_predictor, "(", ch$my_pred_form, ")",
         if (ch$my_copredictor != "none") paste0(" + ", ch$my_copredictor) else "",
         " | ", ch$my_estimator, " | ", ch$my_sample,
         " | w:", ch$my_weights, " | ", ch$my_family)
}

# Where a result sits in the canonical 840. Reported by both the exploratory
# and the declared paths so the two are read on the same scale.
.placement <- function(aligned_r) {
  canon <- .grid[.grid$family == "gaussian" & .grid$predictor == "unemp", ]
  canon_rca <- canon$r * ifelse(canon$positive_outcome, 1, -1)
  100 * mean(canon_rca < aligned_r)
}

# One pre-filled Google Form link, used by both submission paths. `phase`
# rides on the free-text spec field rather than in a field of its own: the
# form schema, the Worker and the sheet are working infrastructure and are
# not worth disturbing for a label. results.qmd reads the prefix back off
# the same field.
.submit_link <- function(ch, hit, phase) {
  fl <- .flip(ch, hit)
  b <- fl * hit$estimate; tv <- fl * hit$statistic; r <- fl * hit$r
  spec_label <- paste0(phase, ": ", .spec_line(ch))

  FORM_ID <- "1FAIpQLSezoAEOnZUfP4pkfN28_XtEBwSyc2RLsXB-h8RPSegF7_t76A"
  field <- c(spec = "entry.832496914", b = "entry.1656311800", se = "entry.1337458262",
             t = "entry.1940779437", df = "entry.1682711955", n = "entry.1586392724",
             r = "entry.1660273001")
  value <- c(spec = spec_label, b = sprintf("%.5f", b),
             se = sprintf("%.5f", hit$se), t = sprintf("%.3f", tv),
             df = as.character(hit$df), n = as.character(hit$n),
             r = sprintf("%.3f", r))
  query <- paste(vapply(names(field), function(k)
    paste0(field[[k]], "=", utils::URLencode(value[[k]], reserved = TRUE)),
    character(1)), collapse = "&")
  list(url = sprintf("https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/%s/viewform?usp=pp_url&%s",
                     FORM_ID, query),
       label = spec_label, b = b, t = tv, r = r, se = hit$se,
       df = hit$df, n = hit$n,
       stat_lab = if (ch$my_family == "beta") "z" else "t")
}

.print_submission <- function(s, lead) {
  cat(lead, "\n\n")
  cat("  spec:", s$label, "\n")
  cat(sprintf("  b = %.5f | se = %.5f | %s = %.3f | df = %d | n = %d | r = %.3f\n\n",
              s$b, s$se, s$stat_lab, s$t, s$df, s$n, s$r))
  cat("Click the link below (or copy the URL) – the form opens with every\n")
  cat("field pre-filled; just press Send.\n\n")
  cat(s$url, "\n")
  htmltools::browsable(htmltools::tags$p(
    htmltools::tags$a(href = s$url, target = "_blank", rel = "noopener",
                      "Open the pre-filled submission form")))
}

# The exploratory log. Every try_spec() call appends a row, so a participant
# who has tried five specifications can print the five side by side and see
# the small multiverse they just built.
.tried <- new.env(parent = emptyenv())
.tried$log <- NULL
.tried$last <- NULL

try_spec <- function(outcome     = "mcosmo",
                     family      = "gaussian",
                     predictor   = "unemp",
                     pred_form   = "raw",
                     copredictor = "none",
                     estimator   = "fe_twoway",
                     sample      = "all",
                     weights     = "none") {
  ch <- .validate(list(my_outcome = outcome, my_family = family,
                       my_predictor = predictor, my_pred_form = pred_form,
                       my_copredictor = copredictor, my_estimator = estimator,
                       my_sample = sample, my_weights = weights), as_args = TRUE)
  hit <- .lookup(ch)
  fl <- .flip(ch, hit)
  aligned_r <- fl * hit$r
  p <- 2 * pt(-abs(hit$statistic), hit$df)
  stat_lab <- if (family == "beta") "z" else "t"

  cat(.spec_line(ch), "\n")
  cat(sprintf("  b = %.5f   se = %.5f   %s = %.3f on %d df   p %s\n",
              fl * hit$estimate, hit$se, stat_lab, fl * hit$statistic, hit$df,
              if (p < 0.001) "< 0.001" else sprintf("= %.3f", p)))
  cat(sprintf("  claim-aligned partial r = %.3f   (below zero supports the claim)\n",
              aligned_r))
  cat(sprintf("  %.1f%% of the canonical 840 support the claim more strongly\n",
              .placement(aligned_r)))

  row <- data.frame(outcome = outcome, family = family, predictor = predictor,
                    pred_form = pred_form, copredictor = copredictor,
                    estimator = estimator, sample = sample, weights = weights,
                    b = fl * hit$estimate, t = fl * hit$statistic,
                    r_aligned = aligned_r,
                    sig = p < 0.05, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  .tried$log <- rbind(.tried$log, row)
  .tried$last <- list(ch = ch, hit = hit)
  invisible(row)
}

my_experiments <- function() {
  if (is.null(.tried$log)) {
    cat("Nothing tried yet – call try_spec() at least once.\n")
    return(invisible(NULL))
  }
  d <- .tried$log
  # Only the axes that actually varied are worth printing; the constant ones
  # are the baseline and repeating them across every row hides the contrast.
  varied <- names(d)[1:8][vapply(d[1:8], function(x) length(unique(x)) > 1,
                                 logical(1))]
  show <- d[, c(varied, "b", "t", "r_aligned", "sig"), drop = FALSE]
  show$b <- signif(show$b, 3); show$t <- round(show$t, 2)
  show$r_aligned <- round(show$r_aligned, 3)
  cat("Specifications you have tried (", nrow(d), "):\n\n", sep = "")
  print(show, row.names = FALSE)
  cat("\nSpread of claim-aligned r: ",
      sprintf("%.3f to %.3f", min(d$r_aligned), max(d$r_aligned)),
      "  |  significant: ", sum(d$sig), " of ", nrow(d), "\n", sep = "")
  invisible(show)
}

submit_exploration <- function() {
  if (is.null(.tried$last))
    stop("Nothing to submit – call try_spec() first, ending with the specification you want on the chart.",
         call. = FALSE)
  s <- .submit_link(.tried$last$ch, .tried$last$hit, "explore")
  .print_submission(s,
    "Your exploratory submission (claim-aligned, the last specification you tried):")
}

prereg <- function() {
  ch <- .check_choices()
  .lookup(ch)   # confirms the combination exists; the result stays unseen
  neg <- ch$my_outcome %in% .neg_framings
  cat("DECLARED – one specification, recorded before seeing its result:\n\n")
  cat("  outcome    :", ch$my_outcome,
      if (neg) "(negative framing – reverse-coded automatically)" else "", "\n")
  cat("  family     :", ch$my_family, "\n")
  cat("  predictor  :", ch$my_predictor, paste0("(", ch$my_pred_form, ")"),
      if (ch$my_predictor == "growth") "(claim-expected sign flipped automatically)" else "", "\n")
  cat("  copredictor:", ch$my_copredictor, "\n")
  cat("  estimator  :", .est_lab(ch$my_estimator), "\n")
  cat("  sample     :", ch$my_sample, "   weights:", ch$my_weights, "\n")
  cat("  claim_align:", isTRUE(claim_align), "\n\n")
  cat("These choices are now fixed for the rest of the session – the later\n")
  cat("cells read them from here. Copy the whole cell into wherever you keep\n")
  cat("your notes: that copy is your preregistration record.\n")
  invisible(ch)
}

build_model <- function(formula, estimator) {
  ch <- .check_choices()
  if (missing(formula) || !inherits(formula, "formula"))
    stop("The first argument must be a formula: outcome ~ predictor terms, unquoted.",
         call. = FALSE)
  lhs <- all.vars(formula[[2]])
  if (!identical(lhs, ch$my_outcome))
    stop(sprintf("Your formula's outcome is '%s' but you preregistered '%s'. The preregistration is binding – fix the formula, not the prereg.",
                 deparse(formula[[2]]), ch$my_outcome), call. = FALSE)
  main <- if (ch$my_predictor == "unemp" && ch$my_pred_form == "log")
    "log(unemp)" else ch$my_predictor
  want <- c(main, if (ch$my_copredictor != "none") ch$my_copredictor)
  got <- attr(terms(formula), "term.labels")
  if (!setequal(got, want))
    stop(sprintf("Right-hand side mismatch: you wrote { %s } but your preregistration implies { %s }.%s",
                 paste(got, collapse = ", "), paste(want, collapse = ", "),
                 if (main == "log(unemp)" && !"log(unemp)" %in% got)
                   " You preregistered the log form – write log(unemp) in the formula." else ""),
         call. = FALSE)
  if (missing(estimator) || !identical(estimator, ch$my_estimator))
    stop(sprintf("estimator = \"%s\" does not match your preregistered \"%s\".",
                 if (missing(estimator)) "" else estimator, ch$my_estimator),
         call. = FALSE)
  cat("Model accepted – it matches your preregistration exactly:\n")
  cat("  ", deparse(formula), ", estimated by ", .est_lab(estimator), "\n", sep = "")
  structure(list(choices = ch, formula = formula, estimator = estimator),
            class = "spec_ticket")
}

run_spec <- function(spec) {
  if (missing(spec) || !inherits(spec, "spec_ticket"))
    stop("Pass the object build_model() returned, e.g. run_spec(my_model).",
         call. = FALSE)
  now <- .check_choices()
  if (!identical(spec$choices, now))
    stop("The preregistration cell has changed since you built this model – rerun prereg() and build_model() so they agree.",
         call. = FALSE)
  ch <- spec$choices
  hit <- .lookup(ch)
  fl <- .flip(ch, hit)
  ca <- isTRUE(claim_align)
  stat_lab <- if (ch$my_family == "beta") "z" else "t"
  b <- hit$estimate; tv <- hit$statistic; r <- hit$r
  if (ca) { b <- fl * b; tv <- fl * tv; r <- fl * r }
  p <- 2 * pt(-abs(hit$statistic), hit$df)
  cat("Your preregistered specification, computed:\n\n")
  cat("  ", .spec_line(ch), "\n", sep = "")
  if (ca && ch$my_outcome %in% .neg_framings)
    cat("  (negative framing – reverse-coded automatically: claim_align = TRUE)\n")
  if (ca && ch$my_predictor == "growth")
    cat("  (growth predictor – sign convention flipped automatically: claim_align = TRUE)\n")
  if (!ca)
    cat("  (claim_align = FALSE: shown on each outcome's own scale; the class chart converts)\n")
  cat(sprintf("\n  b = %.5f   se = %.5f   %s = %.3f on %d df   p %s\n",
              b, hit$se, stat_lab, tv, hit$df,
              if (p < 0.001) "< 0.001" else sprintf("= %.3f", p)))
  aligned_r <- fl * hit$r
  cat(sprintf("  claim-aligned partial r = %.3f   (below zero supports the claim)\n",
              aligned_r))
  canon <- .grid[.grid$family == "gaussian" & .grid$predictor == "unemp", ]
  canon_rca <- canon$r * ifelse(canon$positive_outcome, 1, -1)
  cat(sprintf("\n  Placement: %.1f%% of the canonical 840 specifications support the claim\n",
              100 * mean(canon_rca < aligned_r)))
  cat("  more strongly than this one (the full universe holds 2,520).\n")
  invisible(list(b = b, se = hit$se, stat = tv, df = hit$df, n = hit$n,
                 r = aligned_r))
}

report_result <- function() {
  ch <- .check_choices()
  hit <- .lookup(ch)
  # The class chart lives on the claim-aligned scale, so a submission is
  # always aligned, whatever claim_align displays in the cells above.
  s <- .submit_link(ch, hit, "declared")
  .print_submission(s,
    "Your declared submission (claim-aligned, straight from your preregistration):")
}
```

## Warm-up – three R's, and one impostor {#task-1-concepts-warm-up-while-the-engine-loads}

**Fix the vocabulary before you touch any data.** Three of the four scenarios below are doing one of our three R's – reproducibility, robustness, replicability. The fourth is doing something else entirely. Read all four, then label each one in the code cell.

***Scenario 1:*** This is an example of \_\_\_\_\_\_.

***Scenario 2:*** Is this a case of \_\_\_\_\_\_ or \_\_\_\_\_\_?

***Scenario 3:*** Their conclusion is that the original analysis has failed to \_\_\_\_\_\_.

***Scenario 4:*** The authors' original findings prove \_\_\_\_\_\_.

The engine should be ready by now. 
Fill in the gaps in the code cell below and run it to print your answers back and confirm that R is alive in your browser.

```{webr}
#| exercise: vocab
#| code-overflow: wrap

cat("
  Scenario 1: A reviewer reruns the authors' Stata .do file on the authors' data and gets a *different* coefficient from the one printed in the paper. This is an example of ______ even though what they *tried* to do failed.

  Scenario 2: The analyst uses the authors' submitted replication dataset, but they re-implement the model in R instead of Stata and centre the predictor. Is this a case of ______ or ______?

  Scenario 3: A preregistered team tests the identical hypothesis on a *separate, much larger* dataset chosen to be theoretically equivalent, and gets results that contradict the original. Their conclusion is that the original analysis has failed to ______.

  Scenario 4: Instead of the survey data used by the original authors, another researcher tests the same underlying idea on social-media texts using a machine-learning classifier method that the original never used. To their surprise, the authors' original findings prove ______, and the researcher concludes that they provide a reliable middle-range theory of the phenomenon they investigate.
")

```

:::: {.solution exercise="vocab"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Answers – and the two traps

1.  **reproducibility** – rerunning the same code on the same data. Here it *failed* to match, but the activity is still reproducibility, and 'not reproduced' is the verdict.
2.  arguably still **reproducibility**, in a grey area – re-implementing on the same data in different software is technically a re-computation – but centring the predictor nudges towards **robustness**. Two packages can also implement the same estimator differently, so make sure you know what the function you call is doing.
3.  **replicability** – same question, independent new data chosen to be theoretically equivalent.
4.  **generalisability** – the impostor: new data *and* a new method at once. It is the fourth cell of the matrix, not one of the three we test today.
:::
::::




## Task 2 – Meet the panel {#task-2-get-the-data-and-look-at-it}

The **EU-frames dataset** (`EUframes_cy.csv`) is already loaded for you as `euframes`. It is the country-year panel behind the whole exercise. The copy this page loads is byte-identical to the one published in the analyst's fork on OSF (osf.io/6zqct – "Multi100 \| Teney_EurSocioRev_2016 \| Analyst_C6HJR", main folder), and the official Multi100 archival record sits at osf.io/8rtwe. Route 1 participants download the same file into their Positron workspace; in the browser it is pre-loaded, so you start straight on the analysis.

Run the cell below to inspect the panel. Edit it freely – this is your environment.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
# How many countries, how many years, how big is the panel?
dplyr::glimpse(euframes)

cat("\nCountries:", dplyr::n_distinct(euframes$cntry),
    " Years:", dplyr::n_distinct(euframes$year),

```

You should see **270 rows**, **27 countries**, **10 years** (2004–2013), and 13 columns. The outcome we care about first is `mcosmo`, the mean 'cosmopolitan' framing of the EU in each country-year, on a 0–1 scale. The predictor is `unemp`, the annual unemployment rate. `growth` is annual GDP growth, and `n_cy` counts the survey respondents behind each row. The [codebook](../data/EUframes_cy_codebook.md) describes the other framings and every remaining column.

Now look at the outcome over time, one small panel per country:

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 6
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(euframes, aes(x = year, y = mcosmo)) +
  geom_line(colour = "grey55") +
  geom_point(size = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~ cntry, ncol = 6) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(2004, 2008, 2013)) +
  labs(
    title = "Cosmopolitan EU framing by country, 2004–2013",
    x = NULL, y = "Mean cosmopolitan framing"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9)
```

Most countries drift gently; a few move sharply around the 2009 crisis. That variation – within a country, over time – is exactly what the fixed-effects model in Task 3 uses.

## Task 2, continued – name the estimand, draw the graph {#task-4-estimand-and-dag}

Before fitting anything, say what you are trying to estimate, in words. A template you can adapt:

> The **unit-specific quantity** is the change in a country-year's mean cosmopolitan EU framing associated with a one-point change in that country's unemployment rate. The **target population** is EU member states over 2004–2013. The **aggregation** is the average of those unit-specific effects, holding fixed each country's time-invariant traits and each year's EU-wide shocks.

That last clause is a causal claim, and a directed acyclic graph makes it checkable. A DAG is a picture of what causes what: variables are nodes, arrows run from cause to effect, and the rules of the graph then tell you which variables have to be adjusted for if the arrow you care about is to be read cleanly. Here is the graph this exercise commits to.

```{r}
#| label: dag-reference
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.4
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-cap: "The committed graph: unemployment to framing, with country and year as confounder pairs. The three pale nodes carry no arrows yet."
library(ggdag)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)

ncl_blue <- "#0e3b6a"; orange <- "#E69F00"; grey_mid <- "#848c94"

dag_ref <- dagify(
  framing      ~ unemployment,
  framing      ~ country,
  unemployment ~ country,
  framing      ~ year,
  unemployment ~ year,
  exposure = "unemployment",
  outcome  = "framing",
  coords = list(
    x = c(unemployment = 0, framing = 3, country = 1, year = 2),
    y = c(unemployment = 0, framing = 0, country = 1.4, year = 1.4)))

# dagify() holds edges, so a node with no arrows cannot live in the graph
# object; the three undecided nodes join at the drawing layer instead.
floaters <- tribble(
  ~name,            ~x,   ~y,
  "growth",         0.9, -1.0,
  "bailout",        1.5, -1.2,
  "politicisation", 3.0, -0.95)

roles <- tribble(
  ~name,            ~role,       ~disp,
  "unemployment",   "predictor", "unemp.",
  "framing",        "outcome",   "framing",
  "country",        "adjusted",  "country",
  "year",           "adjusted",  "year",
  "growth",         "candidate", "growth",
  "bailout",        "candidate", "bailout",
  "politicisation", "candidate", "politic.")

dag_tidy <- tidy_dagitty(dag_ref)
update_dag_data(dag_tidy) <- pull_dag_data(dag_tidy) |>
  bind_rows(floaters) |>
  left_join(roles, by = "name") |>
  mutate(role = factor(role, levels = c("predictor", "outcome",
                                        "adjusted", "candidate")))

ggplot(dag_tidy, aes(x = x, y = y, xend = xend, yend = yend)) +
  geom_dag_edges_arc(curvature = 0.18, edge_colour = grey_mid,
                     edge_width = 1.1,
                     arrow = grid::arrow(length = grid::unit(9, "pt"),
                                         type = "closed")) +
  geom_dag_point(aes(fill = role), shape = 21, size = 26, stroke = 0,
                 colour = "white") +
  geom_dag_text(aes(label = disp, colour = role), size = 3.6,
                fontface = "bold") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(predictor = orange, outcome = ncl_blue,
                               adjusted = "#c7ccd2", candidate = "#dde2e7"),
                    guide = "none") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(predictor = "#FFFFFF", outcome = "#FFFFFF",
                                 adjusted = ncl_blue, candidate = "#5d666e"),
                      guide = "none") +
  theme_dag() +
  expand_limits(x = c(-0.5, 3.5), y = c(-1.7, 1.9))
```

Five arrows are drawn. `unemployment -> framing` is the path of interest. Above it, `country` is a common cause of both: stable national traits such as size, EU tenure and labour-market institutions move local unemployment and shape how people frame the EU. `year` does the same job for the EU-wide shocks that hit every country in the same calendar year. The three pale nodes below carry no arrows yet, because whether they belong is a decision you make rather than one the exercise makes for you.

You build the graph yourself in the cells below, in ordinary R. `dagify()` takes one formula per arrow, written the way you write a model, so `framing ~ unemployment` is the arrow that runs *into* `framing`. Read the tilde as 'is caused by' rather than 'is regressed on' and the direction comes out right every time. Because each arrow is a line of R rather than a fragment of a string, an arrow you are unsure about can sit there commented out, and adopting it means deleting a `#`.

`dagify()` and `adjustmentSets()` are ready in this page already, so you can go straight to the next cell. The optional cell below adds the *picture*: it installs `ggdag`, which brings `igraph`, `ggraph` and four further dependencies with it – roughly 23 MB of download, and a noticeable pause on a slow connection. Run it if you want the plot; skip it and everything else in Task 2 still works, because the figure above is the same graph.

```{webr}
#| include: false
#| autorun: true
# Graph machinery for Task 2. The adjustment-set question is answered here in
# base R rather than by dagitty, because dagitty reaches its graph algorithms
# through a JavaScript engine that a browser only exposes to a page served with
# cross-origin isolation headers (COOP and COEP). Without them the call fails
# with a JavaScript type error rather than an R error, so the browser lab
# cannot depend on it. These functions agree with dagitty's `adjustmentSets()`
# on every arrow combination this task offers and on 378 random test graphs.

.dag_has_edge <- function(dag, a, b) any(dag$edges$from == a & dag$edges$to == b)

# A node counts as one of its own descendants, which is what the collider rule
# below needs.
.dag_descendants <- function(dag, v) {
  seen <- v
  frontier <- v
  while (length(frontier)) {
    kids <- setdiff(dag$edges$to[dag$edges$from %in% frontier], seen)
    seen <- c(seen, kids)
    frontier <- kids
  }
  seen
}

# Every simple path between two nodes, ignoring arrow direction. The recursion
# is safe only because a teaching graph is tiny.
.dag_paths <- function(dag, from, to) {
  out <- list()
  neighbours <- function(v) unique(c(dag$edges$to[dag$edges$from == v],
                                     dag$edges$from[dag$edges$to == v]))
  walk <- function(path) {
    v <- path[length(path)]
    if (v == to) {
      out[[length(out) + 1L]] <<- path
      return(invisible(NULL))
    }
    for (w in setdiff(neighbours(v), path)) walk(c(path, w))
  }
  walk(from)
  out
}

# A path is blocked by the set z if any node along it is either a non-collider
# inside z, or a collider with no descendant in z.
.dag_path_blocked <- function(dag, path, z) {
  if (length(path) < 3L) return(FALSE)
  for (i in seq(2L, length(path) - 1L)) {
    node <- path[i]
    collider <- .dag_has_edge(dag, path[i - 1L], node) &&
                .dag_has_edge(dag, path[i + 1L], node)
    if (collider) {
      if (!any(.dag_descendants(dag, node) %in% z)) return(TRUE)
    } else if (node %in% z) {
      return(TRUE)
    }
  }
  FALSE
}

.dagify_builtin <- function(..., exposure = NULL, outcome = NULL,
                            coords = NULL) {
  parts <- lapply(list(...), function(f) {
    child <- all.vars(f[[2]])
    parent <- all.vars(f[[3]])
    data.frame(from = parent, to = rep(child, length(parent)))
  })
  e <- do.call(rbind, parts)
  structure(list(edges = e, exposure = exposure, outcome = outcome,
                 nodes = unique(c(e$from, e$to))),
            class = "simple_dag")
}

# The backdoor criterion, brute-forced over subsets of the eligible variables:
# smallest sets first, and a set is skipped once it contains a set already
# found, which leaves only the minimal ones.
.adjustment_sets_builtin <- function(x, exposure = x$exposure,
                                     outcome = x$outcome, ...) {
  backdoor <- Filter(function(p) .dag_has_edge(x, p[2L], exposure),
                     .dag_paths(x, exposure, outcome))
  candidates <- setdiff(x$nodes, c(outcome, .dag_descendants(x, exposure)))
  found <- list()
  for (k in seq(0L, length(candidates))) {
    subsets <- if (k == 0L) list(character(0)) else
      utils::combn(candidates, k, simplify = FALSE)
    for (z in subsets) {
      if (any(vapply(found, function(f) all(f %in% z), logical(1)))) next
      if (all(vapply(backdoor, function(p) .dag_path_blocked(x, p, z),
                     logical(1)))) {
        found[[length(found) + 1L]] <- sort(z)
      }
    }
  }
  structure(found, class = "simple_dag_sets")
}

print.simple_dag_sets <- function(x, ...) {
  if (!length(x)) {
    cat("(no set of these variables closes every backdoor path)\n")
  } else {
    for (z in x) {
      cat(if (length(z)) paste0("{ ", paste(z, collapse = ", "), " }") else "{}",
          "\n", sep = "")
    }
  }
  invisible(x)
}

# Registered rather than left in the session: these cells do not evaluate in
# the global environment, so plain S3 dispatch would not find the method.
registerS3method("print", "simple_dag_sets", print.simple_dag_sets)

dagify <- .dagify_builtin
adjustmentSets <- .adjustment_sets_builtin
dag_engine <- "built-in"

# Whether dagitty could work here at all. Its JavaScript bridge needs
# SharedArrayBuffer, which a browser grants only to a cross-origin-isolated
# page, and the failure is a JavaScript error that tryCatch() cannot catch – so
# the question has to be asked before anything calls dagitty.
.dagitty_possible <- function() {
  isTRUE(tryCatch(
    as.numeric(webr::eval_js(
      "typeof SharedArrayBuffer === 'undefined' ? 0 : 1")) == 1,
    error = function(e) FALSE))
}
```

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
# Optional: install ggdag so the graph can be drawn. The check comes first,
# because ggdag draws through dagitty and there is no point downloading 23 MB
# that this browser cannot use.
if (!.dagitty_possible()) {
  cat("This page is not served with the headers dagitty's graph engine needs,\nso there is no plot here – the figure above is the same graph.\nEverything else in Task 2 works: the adjustment set uses this page's own graph code.\n")
} else {
  have_ggdag <- tryCatch({
    webr::install("ggdag", quiet = TRUE)
    suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(ggdag))
    TRUE
  }, error = function(e) FALSE)

  if (have_ggdag) {
    dagify <- ggdag::dagify
    adjustmentSets <- dagitty::adjustmentSets
    dag_engine <- "dagitty"
    cat("ggdag is loaded: the graph, the adjustment set and the plot all work.\n")
  } else {
    cat("ggdag did not install. The adjustment set still works – it uses this page's own graph code.\nUse the figure above for the picture.\n")
  }
}
```

Now specify the graph. The five committed arrows are live; the arguable ones are commented out, one substantive claim per line. Uncomment any you believe, then run the cell.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
my_dag <- dagify(
  # The path of interest, and the two confounder pairs two-way fixed effects
  # soak up.
  framing      ~ unemployment,
  framing      ~ country,
  unemployment ~ country,
  framing      ~ year,
  unemployment ~ year,

  # GROWTH as a time-varying confounder: a slump raises unemployment and may
  # sour EU sentiment in the same year.
  # framing      ~ growth,
  # unemployment ~ growth,

  # BAILOUT as a mediator: unemployment triggers a financial-assistance
  # programme, which then shapes framing.
  # bailout ~ unemployment,
  # framing ~ bailout,

  # POLITICISATION of the EU by parties and elites as another cause of
  # framing. Multi100 instructed analysts to disregard it.
  # framing ~ politicisation,

  exposure = "unemployment",
  outcome  = "framing",
  # Coordinates for all seven nodes; the three not currently wired up are
  # simply ignored, so this block never needs editing.
  coords = list(
    x = c(unemployment = 0, framing = 3, country = 1, year = 2,
          growth = 0.9, bailout = 1.5, politicisation = 3),
    y = c(unemployment = 0, framing = 0, country = 1.4, year = 1.4,
          growth = -1.0, bailout = -1.2, politicisation = -0.95)))

adjustmentSets(my_dag)
```

With the five committed arrows the minimal adjustment set is `{ country, year }` – exactly what a two-way fixed-effects model absorbs. Country fixed effects adjust for `country` and year fixed effects adjust for `year`, so the model you fitted in Task 3 and the graph you just wrote are one identification claim in two languages.

Now uncomment the growth pair and run the cell again. The set becomes `{ country, growth, year }`, because a slump varies within a country over time and fixed effects only remove country-constant and year-common variation. Nothing in the Task 3 model reaches it, and your specification would need `growth` as a co-predictor to match your beliefs – a choice waiting for you on the menu in Task 5. The bailout arrows behave differently. A mediator sits on the path you are trying to measure, so the adjustment set does not grow when you add one; adjusting for it would strip out part of the very effect you are after.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4
# Drawing needs both the ggdag install and dagitty's own engine; where either
# is missing the figure at the top of this task stands in.
if (identical(dag_engine, "dagitty")) {
  print(ggdag::ggdag_classic(my_dag, size = 4) + ggdag::theme_dag())
} else {
  cat("No plot here – scroll up to the reference figure, which is this same graph.\n")
}
```

Write two sentences for your own notes. What do two-way fixed effects adjust for, and what can they **not** fix? (Hint: anything time-varying within a country that you have not measured.)


## Task 3 – Reproduce the recorded result

This is the **reproducibility** check. Fit the two-way fixed-effects model the Multi100 Task-2 constraints point to:

```
mcosmo ~ unemp_c   with fixed effects for country and year
```

where `unemp_c` is the unemployment rate centred on its grand mean. The target is **t = −3.804** (df = 233, N = 270) – the value on record for analyst C6HJR in the Multi100 dataset.

The cell below is an exercise. Replace the blanks (`______`) with the missing code, then press "Run Code". If you get stuck, open the hints below; the solution has the full code.

```{webr}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: reproduce
euframes <- read.csv("data/EUframes_cy.csv")
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: reproduce
# 1. centre the unemployment rate on its grand mean
euframes$unemp_c <- euframes$unemp - ______

# 2. fit two-way fixed effects with fixest::feols
#    the part after the | adds the fixed effects
m1 <- feols(mcosmo ~ unemp_c | ______, data = euframes)

broom::tidy(m1)
```

:::: {.hint exercise="reproduce"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint 1 – centring

To centre a variable on its grand mean, subtract the mean of the whole column:

``` r
euframes$unemp_c <- euframes$unemp - mean(euframes$unemp)
```

With fixed effects present this does not change the t-statistic, but it is the transformation the constrained specification asks for, so do it explicitly.
:::
::::

:::: {.hint exercise="reproduce"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint 2 – the fixed-effects syntax

In `fixest::feols`, the bar `|` separates the regression from the fixed effects. To add country and year fixed effects, list them after the bar separated by `+`:

``` r
feols(mcosmo ~ unemp_c | cntry + year, data = euframes)
```
:::
::::

:::: {.solution exercise="reproduce"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Fully worked solution

``` r
euframes$unemp_c <- euframes$unemp - mean(euframes$unemp)
m1 <- feols(mcosmo ~ unemp_c | cntry + year, data = euframes)
broom::tidy(m1)
```

You should get `estimate ≈ −0.00347`, `std.error ≈ 0.00091`, `statistic ≈ −3.80` – the recorded value reproduces from the published data and the published model. `feols` reports IID standard errors by default when two fixed-effect dimensions are present, which is why it matches the `plm` value to three decimals.
:::
::::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Everyone gets the same number, and the five analysts still disagreed

You reproduced the recorded value exactly, and so did everyone else in the room, because everyone ran the same code on the same file – which is why reproducibility is the cheap R.

The five Multi100 analysts each wrote their own code for the same claim, and came back with five different answers, one of them not significant. Their pipelines are competent, well-organised work, so the spread is not a quality problem. It is what happens when a claim stated in words leaves several genuinely defensible quantities on the table, and different analysts estimate different ones without noticing they have chosen.

Task 2 named the quantity you are after and drew the graph your adjustment set follows from. Task 4 now shows you how far the answer moves when the other choices move.
:::

## Task 4 – Work the menu {#task-4-explore}

This task is **exploration, and it is meant to be**. You are going to try several specifications, see what each one does, and get a feel for which choices move the estimate and which barely touch it. Nothing here is a commitment; that comes in Task 5.

`try_spec()` takes one argument per axis of the [specification menu](spec-menu.qmd), and every argument already carries the baseline you just reproduced. So changing one thing means changing one argument, and everything you do not name stays at baseline.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
# The baseline, with nothing changed - this is the specification you
# reproduced in Task 3.
try_spec()
```

Now change one axis at a time. Each of the four calls below moves exactly one thing; run them, and watch which ones matter.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
try_spec(outcome   = "mpos")        # the composite of all positive framings
try_spec(estimator = "pooled_cl")   # no country comparison absorbed at all
try_spec(sample    = "no_bailout")  # drop the assistance-programme countries
try_spec(weights   = "n_cy")        # weight cells by how many people are in them
```

Then try your own combinations. The full set of arguments, with the baseline as the default for each:

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
try_spec(
  outcome     = "mcosmo",     # mcosmo | mutil | mpos | mcomm | mlib | mneg
  family      = "gaussian",   # gaussian | beta
  predictor   = "unemp",      # unemp | growth
  pred_form   = "raw",        # raw | log   (growth: raw only)
  copredictor = "none",       # none | growth | unemp
  estimator   = "fe_twoway",  # fe_twoway | fe_country | re | pooled_cl
  sample      = "all",        # all | y2004_2008 | y2009_2013 | no_bailout | no_GR_ES
  weights     = "none"        # none | n_cy   (re is never weighted)
)
```

Everything you try is logged. Print the log to see the small multiverse you have just built – only the axes you actually varied are shown, so the contrast is readable:

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
my_experiments()
```

When you have tried three or four, decide which one you would defend if you had to, run it once more so it is the most recent, and submit it. It lands on the live [Multiverse]({{< var live-results-url >}}) chart as an **exploratory** result:

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
submit_exploration()
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Why 'exploratory'?

Because you chose this specification after seeing what several specifications do, so it cannot carry the guarantee that a declared choice carries – no one can rule out that it might have been chosen *because* of its result. This is something we almost never know in case of published papers, unless their analysis had been pre-registered and departures from the pre-registration documented. In this workshop exploration is a natural step, but you'll also practice pre-registering your chosen analysis; you will submit twice: once here, and once in Task 5.
:::

## Task 5 – Commit before you look {#task-5-my-preregistration}

The point of preregistration is that you commit to a choice **before** you see what it does. It stops you quietly picking the specification that happens to give the answer you wanted. Here the commitment binds mechanically as well: the session remembers the choices you declare in this cell, and every later cell reads them from here. The model builder refuses code that departs from them.

::: {.callout-important icon="false"}
## The block is a real preregistration, shortened

*Each numbered comment maps to a question in the OSF "Preregistration Template from AsPredicted.org" (the eight-question short form). Because you are reanalysing data that already exist, field 2 also stands in for the prior-knowledge section of the secondary-data template (van den Akker et al. 2021) – the part AsPredicted leaves out.*
:::

Make one choice on each axis of the [specification menu](spec-menu.qmd), complete the dotted lines, then run the cell. Every axis is live, the outcome family and the predictor included. `claim_align <- TRUE` is the day's convention, applied automatically: negative framings are reverse-coded (1 − y) and growth's claim-expected sign is flipped, so 'supports the claim' reads as a negative sign for everyone.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
# ============================================================================
# MY PREREGISTRATION – one specification, declared before seeing its result
# ============================================================================
# 1. The claim I am testing: .................................................
# 2. The data + what I already know: EUframes_cy.csv (270 country-years,
#    public); I know the constrained baseline gives t = -3.804.
# 3. My one specification – one choice on each axis:

my_outcome     <- "mcosmo"     # mcosmo | mutil | mpos    (positive framings)
                               # mcomm  | mlib  | mneg    (negative framings)
my_family      <- "gaussian"   # gaussian | beta   (logit-link on the cell
                               #                    means; beta reports z)
my_predictor   <- "unemp"      # unemp | growth    (the claim-carrying measure)
my_pred_form   <- "raw"        # raw | log   (growth: raw only; centring or
                               #              z-scaling would leave t, r and p
                               #              unchanged, not separate analyses)
my_copredictor <- "none"       # none | growth (beside unemp) | unemp (beside growth)
my_estimator   <- "fe_twoway"  # fe_twoway | fe_country | re | pooled_cl
my_sample      <- "all"        # all | y2004_2008 | y2009_2013 | no_bailout | no_GR_ES
my_weights     <- "none"       # none | n_cy   (re is never weighted)

claim_align    <- TRUE         # the day's convention, applied automatically

# 4. Why these controls, in one DAG-grounded sentence: .......................
# 5. Supported if the claim-aligned coefficient is negative and p < .05;
#    undermined if non-significant or positive. I will report what I get.

prereg()   # checks every choice against the menu and records the declaration
```

An optional mirror form logs preregistrations for the room, and the link is shared in the session. It is not required. The cell above, copied into your notes, is your preregistration record.



## Task 5, continued – build, run and report {#task-5-build-run-report}

This is the **robustness** check, and it is the part your classmates cannot copy from you: together the room samples the multiverse of defensible analyses. You have declared your specification. Now translate it into model syntax yourself, filling the three gaps – the outcome, the right-hand side, and the estimator code – exactly as you preregistered them. `build_model()` knows your declaration and accepts nothing else, and its error messages tell you what is off. Write the log form as `log(unemp)`, and add any co-predictor with `+`.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
my_model <- build_model(______ ~ ______, estimator = "______")
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint – from menu speak to model syntax

The formula uses the column names of `euframes`: the outcome you preregistered on the left of `~`, the predictor terms on the right. For the baseline declaration it is `mcosmo ~ unemp`; with the log form it would be `mcosmo ~ log(unemp)`; with a co-predictor, `mcosmo ~ unemp + growth`. The estimator is the menu code itself, in quotes: `"fe_twoway"`, `"fe_country"`, `"re"` or `"pooled_cl"`. You do not write the fixed-effects or clustering syntax here – the estimator code stands for it, and Task 3 showed what it expands to.
:::

When the model is accepted, run it. Every specification on the menu is pre-computed in the committed grid – the same numbers a live fit produces, without downloading the heavier estimation packages into your browser:

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
run_spec(my_model)
```

Read the output like an analyst: the coefficient and its claim-aligned partial *r* (below zero supports the claim), and your placement – what share of the canonical 840-specification grid supports the claim more strongly than your choice does. The five Multi100 analysts run from about the 16th percentile (the most strongly claim-supporting) to about the 68th (near the null), and your dot is about to join theirs.

Now send it to the room. There is nothing to fill in and nothing to transcribe – the result travels from your declaration. The cell prints your submission line and a pre-filled form link; click it and press **Send**. Your dot joins the live [Multiverse]({{< var live-results-url >}}) chart within seconds, this time labelled **declared** rather than exploratory.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
report_result()
```

If the form will not open on your machine, read the printed numbers to the facilitator and your dot still lands.

**A second declared specification?** Edit the preregistration cell, rerun `prereg()`, rebuild, rerun. The mechanics allow it, and the label does not change – so be clear with yourself about what the second one is. Your first declaration was made without knowing its result. Anything after it was not, which puts it back in the same category as Task 4, and you should say so when you report it.
